triage.name: Primary open-angle glaucoma
triage.reason: Asymptomatic progressive vision loss found on exam and screening; a student can reach it from risk factors, optic disc exam and tonometry.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Decreased contrast sensitivity' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Extraocular movements normal' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Temporal artery tenderness' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Neurological examination normal' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common and more severe in people of African ancestry, who also tend to present at a younger age
Leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide
Prevalence rises steadily with age after 40
Hispanic and Latino older adults have higher rates than White older adults

risk_factors.text: Family history of glaucoma in a first-degree relative
Corticosteroid use, especially prolonged topical or systemic
Optic disc hemorrhage or large cup-to-disc ratio

family_history: Glaucoma in a parent or sibling
Blindness in a relative attributed to glaucoma
social_history: Limited access to routine eye care
exposures: Long-term topical or systemic corticosteroid use

chief_complaints.text: I don't have any eye symptoms — my eye doctor found something at my routine exam
I've been bumping into things on my right side and didn't realize it
My side vision seems narrower than it used to be
It feels like I'm looking through a tunnel

hpi.onset: Insidious; typically no symptoms at all until optic nerve damage is advanced
hpi.duration: Present for years before it is noticed; often detected on a routine eye exam
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive and painless; peripheral vision is lost first, and central vision is affected only late in the disease
hpi.location: Both eyes, though often asymmetric; peripheral vision before central vision
hpi.quality: Painless loss of side vision; may be described as missing objects on one side, bumping into things, or a narrowed field
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at detection; functionally severe once central vision is involved
hpi.timing: Constant and slowly worsening over months to years

associated_symptoms.text: Difficulty seeing at night or in dim light
Blurred vision that comes and goes
Difficulty with glare or driving at night

pertinent_negatives: Nausea or vomiting with eye symptoms
Curtain over part of the vision

negatives: Transient visual loss like a curtain coming down

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or cataracts, and field loss is often advanced before it is recognized; falls and difficulty driving may be the first clue.
missing_classic_features: Clear report of peripheral vision loss

atypical.how_it_differs: Visual complaints may be attributed to diabetic retinopathy, and both conditions can coexist, so the field loss is often overlooked.
missing_classic_features: Isolated glaucoma explanation for vision change

atypical.how_it_differs: Primary open-angle glaucoma is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually part of a juvenile-onset or secondary form and may present with eye rubbing, tearing, photophobia or poor school performance.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; vision complaints may be absent
general.moderate: Comfortable; may report trouble with side vision or driving
general.severe: Comfortable but functionally limited; may bump into objects on one side
general.critical: No acute distress; advanced bilateral field loss with impaired mobility

findings.maneuver: Perform a dilated fundoscopic exam and inspect the optic disc for cupping and rim thinning
findings.finding: Enlarged cup-to-disc ratio with thinning of the neuroretinal rim, often asymmetric between eyes
Intraocular pressure above the normal range, typically 22–40 mm Hg; may be normal in normal-tension glaucoma

findings.maneuver: Perform confrontational visual field testing or formal perimetry
findings.finding: Peripheral visual field loss, often an arcuate scotoma or nasal step

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart
findings.finding: Reduced visual acuity, usually preserved until late disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the optic disc margins on dilated fundoscopy
findings.finding: Splinter hemorrhage at the optic disc margin
Relative afferent pupillary defect in asymmetric disease

findings.maneuver: Measure central corneal thickness with pachymetry
findings.finding: Thin central cornea, which affects the accuracy of tonometry

findings.maneuver: Perform gonioscopy to assess the anterior chamber angle
findings.finding: Open anterior chamber angle without peripheral anterior synechiae

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in room light
findings.finding: No conjunctival injection or ciliary flush

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a slit lamp
findings.finding: Clear cornea without epithelial edema or microcystic changes

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow a target in all directions of gaze
findings.finding: Full, conjugate extraocular movements without pain or diplopia
No tenderness, thickening or nodularity of the temporal arteries

findings.maneuver: Test cranial nerves, strength, sensation and coordination
findings.finding: Nonfocal neurologic examination without motor, sensory or cerebellar deficits

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer

findings.text: Thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer, most often in the superior and inferior arcuate regions
Reduced ganglion cell complex thickness on macular scans
Progressive thinning compared with prior scans, confirming progression
Enlarged cup-to-disc ratio with thinning of the neuroretinal rim
Disc asymmetry between the two eyes
Splinter hemorrhage at the disc margin
Bayoneting or nasal displacement of the retinal vessels
Arcuate scotoma respecting the horizontal midline
Tunnel or central island of vision remaining in advanced disease

imaging.study: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy
imaging.preferred_when: The angle cannot be assessed by gonioscopy or a secondary cause is suspected

findings.text: Open anterior chamber angle without iridotrabecular contact

imaging.study: CT or MRI of the brain and orbits
imaging.preferred_when: Atypical features suggest a neurologic or compressive cause of optic neuropathy

findings.text: No intracranial mass, chiasmal lesion or optic nerve compression

initial.why: Measures intraocular pressure, the main modifiable risk factor
Assesses the optic disc for cupping, rim thinning and hemorrhage
Confirms the anterior chamber angle is open and excludes angle-closure
Documents and stages the characteristic peripheral field loss

initial.test: Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer
initial.why: Provides an objective baseline of nerve fiber layer thickness for tracking progression
Central corneal thickness affects the accuracy of tonometry and risk estimates
Looks for secondary causes such as pigment dispersion, pseudoexfoliation or uveitis

confirmatory.why: Creates a permanent baseline record of the disc for comparison over time

confirmatory.test: Repeat automated visual field perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2)
confirmatory.why: A second field confirms a reproducible defect and reduces testing artifact
confirmatory.only_if: the first visual field is abnormal or unreliable

supporting.why: Diabetes is a risk factor and affects overall vascular risk
Thyroid eye disease can rarely mimic or contribute to optic nerve findings
Screens for giant cell arteritis when the presentation is atypical
supporting.only_if: the patient is over 50 with atypical optic neuropathy, headache or systemic symptoms

supporting.why: Adds to ESR in the evaluation for giant cell arteritis
supporting.only_if: the patient is over 50 with atypical optic neuropathy, headache or systemic symptoms

not_indicated.why: No role in the diagnosis of open-angle glaucoma
No role in the diagnosis of open-angle glaucoma
Not relevant to the diagnostic workup of glaucoma

not_indicated.test: CT or MRI of the brain and orbits
not_indicated.why: Reserved for atypical features suggesting a neurologic cause
not_indicated.only_if: atypical optic neuropathy, rapid progression or neurologic symptoms are present

decision_points: Confirm the anterior chamber angle is open by gonioscopy before diagnosing open-angle glaucoma
A single elevated intraocular pressure reading is not diagnostic; combine pressure, disc appearance and visual field findings
Normal intraocular pressure does not exclude glaucoma (normal-tension glaucoma)
Repeat visual fields and imaging over time to distinguish true progression from test variability
Consider giant cell arteritis in older patients with atypical or sudden optic neuropathy

criteria.name: Diagnosis of primary open-angle glaucoma
criteria.summary: An open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy together with characteristic optic nerve damage (cupping, rim thinning or nerve fiber layer loss) and a matching visual field defect, in the absence of another explanation. Intraocular pressure is often but not always elevated.
items: Open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy
Optic disc cupping or retinal nerve fiber layer thinning
Reproducible visual field defect consistent with the disc findings
No secondary cause of optic neuropathy identified

differential.name: Primary angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Both cause optic nerve damage and visual field loss, and both are called glaucoma; the angle is the key distinction.
differential.trigger: Severe eye pain, red eye, headache, halos, nausea or vomiting with blurred vision, or a shallow anterior chamber on exam.

history: Sudden onset of severe eye pain
Headache, nausea or vomiting with the eye symptoms
Halos around lights
Attacks triggered by dim light, stress or anticholinergic medicines
exam: Red eye with ciliary flush
Corneal edema and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
Shallow anterior chamber on slit lamp
Closed or occludable angle on gonioscopy
Intraocular pressure often markedly elevated, above 40 mm Hg
imaging: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy showing iridotrabecular contact

differential.name: Normal-tension glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Identical optic disc cupping and visual field loss but intraocular pressure is within the normal range.

history: No eye pain or redness
Similar insidious peripheral vision loss
May have a history of migraine, Raynaud phenomenon or nocturnal hypotension
exam: Optic disc cupping and rim thinning
Intraocular pressure consistently 21 mm Hg or lower on repeated measurements
Open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy
labs: No laboratory finding distinguishes it; workup is aimed at excluding other optic neuropathies
imaging: Optical coherence tomography shows retinal nerve fiber layer thinning
Visual field defects may be more central or paracentral than in primary open-angle glaucoma

differential.name: Optic neuritis
differential.why_considered: Causes optic nerve dysfunction with visual loss and can be mistaken for glaucoma when the disc appears abnormal.
differential.trigger: Subacute painful loss of vision, especially with eye movement, in a younger patient.

history: Pain with eye movement
Rapid onset over hours to days
Central vision loss rather than peripheral field loss
May have prior neurologic symptoms suggesting demyelinating disease
exam: Reduced color vision out of proportion to acuity
Relative afferent pupillary defect
Disc may be swollen rather than cupped
Visual field defect often central or cecocentral
labs: May have abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings if demyelinating disease is suspected
imaging: MRI of the brain and orbits may show optic nerve enhancement or demyelinating lesions

differential.name: Ischemic optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Causes sudden painless visual loss with optic disc swelling or pallor, and can be confused with glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
differential.trigger: Sudden painless visual loss in an older adult, especially with headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness.

history: Sudden onset of visual loss, often noticed on waking
Headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or polymyalgia symptoms in giant cell arteritis
May have systemic vascular risk factors
exam: Diffuse or sectoral disc swelling acutely, followed by pallor
Visual field defect often altitudinal
No significant cupping in the acute phase
labs: Elevated ESR and CRP in giant cell arteritis
imaging: Temporal artery biopsy may confirm giant cell arteritis
MRI may show optic nerve enhancement

differential.name: Diabetic retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Common cause of visual loss in adults with diabetes and can coexist with glaucoma, leading to attribution of visual symptoms to one condition.

history: Known diabetes mellitus
Blurred vision that fluctuates with glucose control
No peripheral field loss early on
exam: Microaneurysms, dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots
Neovascularization in proliferative disease
Optic disc may be normal or show only mild cupping
imaging: Optical coherence tomography may show macular edema
Fluorescein angiography shows leakage and capillary nonperfusion

differential.name: Cataract
differential.why_considered: Very common cause of gradual painless visual decline in older adults and often coexists with glaucoma.

history: Gradual blurring of vision, often worse at night or with glare
Difficulty reading in dim light
No peripheral field loss
exam: Lens opacity on slit lamp examination
Normal optic disc and intraocular pressure
Normal visual fields

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Can cause peripheral visual field loss and is a sight-threatening emergency.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of flashes, floaters or a curtain-like shadow across the vision.

history: Sudden onset of flashes and floaters
Curtain or shadow over part of the vision
May have recent trauma or eye surgery
exam: Reduced visual acuity if the macula is involved
Visual field defect corresponding to the detached retina
Retinal tear or detachment seen on dilated fundoscopy
imaging: Ocular ultrasound if the view is obscured

differential.name: Pituitary adenoma with chiasmal compression
differential.why_considered: Causes bilateral peripheral visual field loss that can be mistaken for glaucomatous field loss.
differential.trigger: Bitemporal visual field loss, headache, or endocrine symptoms such as amenorrhea or galactorrhea.

history: Bitemporal field loss, often noticed as bumping into things on both sides
Headache
Endocrine symptoms such as amenorrhea, galactorrhea, or acromegaly
exam: Bitemporal hemianopia on visual field testing
Optic disc may be normal or pale, not cupped
Normal intraocular pressure
labs: Elevated prolactin or other pituitary hormone abnormalities
imaging: MRI of the brain showing a sellar or suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm

severity.mild: Early disease: optic disc cupping and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning with a mild or no reproducible visual field defect; intraocular pressure may be mildly elevated; the patient is asymptomatic.
severity.moderate: Established disease: clear glaucomatous optic neuropathy with a reproducible arcuate scotoma or nasal step; the patient may notice difficulty with side vision or driving.
severity.severe: Advanced disease: marked cupping, dense visual field loss encroaching on fixation, reduced visual acuity, and functional limitation with mobility and reading.
severity.critical: Not applicable; primary open-angle glaucoma is not life-threatening, but it can cause irreversible blindness if untreated.

red_flags.finding: Severe eye pain, red eye, headache, nausea or vomiting with blurred vision
red_flags.meaning: Suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma, not open-angle glaucoma; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation.
Suggests vascular or ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal detachment, or another emergency; needs urgent evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Flashes, floaters, or a curtain over the vision
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal detachment; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive visual field loss over days to weeks
red_flags.meaning: Atypical for primary open-angle glaucoma; consider compressive, inflammatory, or ischemic causes.

red_flags.finding: Visual loss with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or headache in a patient over 50
red_flags.meaning: Suggests giant cell arteritis; needs urgent evaluation and treatment to prevent bilateral blindness.

complications.name: Irreversible peripheral vision loss
clues: Progressive arcuate scotoma or nasal step on perimetry
Retinal nerve fiber layer thinning on optical coherence tomography

complications.name: Central vision loss and legal blindness
Falls and motor vehicle collisions from field loss
clues: Bumping into objects on one side

complications.name: Depression and reduced quality of life

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are often attributed to normal aging or cataract; field loss may be advanced before it is recognized, and falls or driving difficulty may be the first clue. Treatment adherence and drop instillation can be challenging.
Visual complaints may be attributed to diabetic retinopathy, and both conditions can coexist; intraocular pressure may be affected by medications and glycemic control.
Primary open-angle glaucoma is uncommon in pregnancy; management must consider the safety of intraocular pressure-lowering medications and the effects of pregnancy on intraocular pressure.
Primary open-angle glaucoma is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually juvenile-onset or secondary and may present with eye rubbing, tearing, photophobia, or poor school performance.

key_questions.question: What eye symptoms have you noticed — any loss of side vision, bumping into things, or a narrowed field?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless, insidious peripheral visual field loss; often no symptoms at all until advanced

key_questions.question: When did you first notice these changes, and have they been getting worse over months or years?
key_questions.looking_for: Slow, progressive course over years rather than sudden onset

key_questions.question: Do you have any eye pain, redness, headache, halos around lights, or nausea with your vision changes?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma or another emergency

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden loss of vision, flashes, floaters, or a curtain over part of your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests retinal detachment or vascular optic neuropathy

key_questions.question: When was your last comprehensive eye exam, and did the eye doctor mention eye pressure or optic nerve changes?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior elevated intraocular pressure, optic disc cupping, or a recommendation for glaucoma follow-up

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family been diagnosed with glaucoma or lost vision from it?
key_questions.looking_for: Glaucoma in a first-degree relative, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you ever used steroid eye drops, steroid pills, or steroid injections, and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged topical or systemic corticosteroid use, which can raise intraocular pressure

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or high nearsightedness?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors that raise suspicion

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble seeing at night, in dim light, or with glare while driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Reduced contrast sensitivity and nyctalopia, common early functional complaints

key_questions.question: How is your vision for reading and for seeing things off to the side?
key_questions.looking_for: Preserved central vision with impaired peripheral vision

key_questions.question: Do you have any trouble with balance, falls, or driving because of your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Functional impact of field loss, especially in older adults

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and how often do you have access to routine eye care?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and limited eye care access as risk and barrier factors

reasoning_points: Insidious, painless, progressive loss of peripheral vision with preserved central vision until late
No red eye, eye pain, headache, halos, or nausea, which argues against angle-closure glaucoma
Risk factors such as older age, African ancestry, family history of glaucoma, diabetes, hypertension, high myopia, or prolonged corticosteroid use
Optic disc cupping with thinning of the neuroretinal rim on dilated fundoscopy, often asymmetric
Intraocular pressure often elevated but may be normal, so a normal pressure does not exclude the diagnosis
Open anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy, which distinguishes it from angle-closure glaucoma
Reproducible visual field defect such as an arcuate scotoma or nasal step matching the disc findings
Optical coherence tomography showing retinal nerve fiber layer thinning supporting glaucomatous optic neuropathy
Exclusion of look-alikes such as optic neuritis, ischemic optic neuropathy, diabetic retinopathy, cataract, retinal detachment, and chiasmal compression

easy: Older adult with a family history of glaucoma found to have elevated intraocular pressure on routine screening
Classic optic disc cupping with an enlarged cup-to-disc ratio on dilated fundoscopy
Asymptomatic patient with a reproducible arcuate scotoma on perimetry
Open angle on gonioscopy with no red eye or pain
medium: Patient reports bumping into objects on one side but has no eye pain or redness
Normal intraocular pressure with disc cupping and field loss suggesting normal-tension glaucoma
Older adult whose visual complaints are attributed to cataract, with glaucoma found on exam
Patient with diabetes whose field loss is initially attributed to diabetic retinopathy
hard: Asymmetric disease with a relative afferent pupillary defect and only subtle disc changes
Advanced field loss discovered after a fall or driving difficulty in an older adult
Patient on long-term corticosteroids with elevated intraocular pressure and early disc changes
Atypical presentation with rapid progression or neurologic symptoms requiring exclusion of compressive or ischemic causes
